searchText: <n0ble> @dankrad regarding pre_state_root proposal. could you please explain, why a simple check that sum(basic_tx_cost) does not exceed the gas limit of a block is not enough? <dankrad> what's basic_tx_cost? <n0ble> probably not the best name, i was referring to basic tx fee (21000/53000) plus fee for tx bytes <dankrad> because then you can create blocks that exceed the gas limit? <n0ble> right, but what stops miner from doing it right now? <dankrad> oh right now a block that exceeds the gas limit is simply invalid and will be discarded <dankrad> but the problem is, my proposal relies on being able to check that a block is valid *before* executing it <dankrad> but you can't determine how much gas it consumes before executing it <n0ble> this is what I am missing (re @dankrad: oh right now a block that exceeds the gas limit is simply invalid and will be discarded) <dankrad> Do you understand it now? <n0ble> I am trying to understand how critical it is. Because charging proposer introduces a restriction on how the block could be produced. According to current model, validator is able to outsource block production to a service or anyone other party; but if proposer becomes responsible for blocks that exceeds the gas limit it doesn’t seem viable to outsource block production in a trustless fashion. <dankrad> It is unfortunately critical for the current Ethereum fee model <dankrad> What we can do is to charge an Eth1 address instead, but a signature from that address (of the whole block) would have to be added to make sure that you can't steal <dankrad> it's not too complex, and we could even provide both options <dankrad> I think of the executable beacon chain to be a temporary solution that should only last 0.5-1.5 years, basically until we can achieve statelessness. The question is how relevant block production outsourcing will become in that timeframe? <dankrad> In a way, it would be better if it isn't too common, because that might mean that people stop running their own Eth1 nodes, which would really compromise the security <vbuterin> > The question is how relevant block production outsourcing will become in that timeframe? <vbuterin> It's relevant already <vbuterin> Flashbots is producing something like 2% of blocks <n0ble> if we have weak statelessness, outsourcing will be still relevant, right? (re @dankrad: I think of the executable beacon chain to be a temporary solution that should only last 0.5-1.5 years, basically until we can achieve statelessness. The question is how relevant block production outsourcing will become in that timeframe?) <vbuterin> (which of course should be read with the same connotation with regard to future trends as "the coronavirus has something like 200 total cases") (re @vbuterin: Flashbots is producing something like 2% of blocks) <n0ble> there should be an equilibrium between cost of running own eth1 node and transaction fees that the owner of the node can make. It’s a centralisation risk of course. But I believe staking pools will run their own eth1 nodes while home stakers would rather outsource eth1 node responsibilities to someone else. The latter also contributes to the promise of running validator on average laptop and raspberri pi (re @dankrad: In a way, it would be better if it isn't too common, because that might mean that people stop running their own Eth1 nodes, which would really compromise the security) <n0ble> 😆 (re @vbuterin: (which of course should be read with the same connotation with regard to future trends as "the coronavirus has something like 200 total cases")) <dankrad> Very relevant, but at that point we would change it to be a shard, and then it would probably be the right decision to go to post-state roots (re @n0ble: if we have weak statelessness, outsourcing will be still relevant, right?) <dankrad> The problem is that for the executable beacon chain, we want *every* staker to run an Eth1 node, otherwise security will really be much worse (because we can get a majority chain on an incorrect Eth1 state transition otherwise, and we don't even have fraud proofs to stop it) Being a block producer is currently the only upside to actually doing this, so if that gets removed by outsourcing being common, we lose a lot of security This is different once we have weak statelessness, because then running the Eth1 node will be cheap (only need to verify a block every now and then, not maintain state); and producing blocks will be much more expensive (need to run a stateful Eth1 node), so outsourcing makes a lot of sense and won't compromise security (re @n0ble: there should be an equilibrium between cost of running own eth1 node and transaction fees that the owner of the node can make. It’s a centralisation risk of course. But I believe staking pools will run their own eth1 nodes while home stakers would rather outsource eth1 node responsibilities to someone else. The latter also contributes to the promise of running validator on average laptop and raspberri pi) <dankrad> Do you not worry that if this becomes the norm, the executable beacon chain merge might result in a real loss of security even compared to Eth1, because once less than 50% of validators verify Eth1 payload, there is a real chance of an invalid Eth1 block being on the majority fork or even finalized? (re @vbuterin: (which of course should be read with the same connotation with regard to future trends as "the coronavirus has something like 200 total cases")) <vbuterin> hmm <vbuterin> perhaps we just need to start working on a proof of custody for EVM execution? <dankrad> that would be the alternative, indeed <dankrad> but another annoying roadblock before the merge <vbuterin> It could be done after the merge, no? <vbuterin> "functionality features earlier, security features later" <dankrad> wait, how can we do the custody without statelessness? <dankrad> doesn't it effectively require fraud proofs as well? <vbuterin> If we have stateless execution we have fraud proofs, no? <dankrad> that's what I am saying. I'm not worried if we have fraud proofs. The problem is for now we won't <dankrad> But is it ok to reduce the security of Eth1 with the merge? Sounds terrible (re @vbuterin: "functionality features earlier, security features later") <vbuterin> ok, so I guess we could just not implement the code for stateless verification until we have the PoC? <dankrad> I'm confused? <vbuterin> me too..... <dankrad> We are talking about post-merge, pre-statelessness <vbuterin> If you can't verify statelessly then you have to process every block, because otherwise you can *only* create flashbots blocks <dankrad> yes <vbuterin> Even the flashbots users don't actually make *every* block be a flashbots block; sometimes flashbots just doesn't come up with anything good <dankrad> what I worry about is that people will just not verify <vbuterin> So there is still an incentive to process the chain to maintain state <n0ble> We can’t prevent outsourcing eth1 node responsibilities from happen, right? Block verification sounds even easier than block production <dankrad> say only 30% of validators run their own Eth1 node, the rest rely on outsourcing. Now a block with an invalid Eth1 state transition will automatically get finalized <dankrad> nothing there to stop it. the attack is trivial <vbuterin> Ah, so I'm saying that even if you "rely on outsourcing" you want to keep an updated state because sometimes the outsourcer doesn't give you anything <n0ble> you assume that outsourcers are all byzantine, right? or there is one outsourcer that is byzantine (re @dankrad: say only 30% of validators run their own Eth1 node, the rest rely on outsourcing. Now a block with an invalid Eth1 state transition will automatically get finalized) <dankrad> why would the outsourcer not give you anything? <vbuterin> well that's just what flashbots does today; it's a specialized outsourcer <dankrad> It doesn't even need to be an oursourcer. Anyone producing a block can now just add a block with an invalid state transition (re @n0ble: you assume that outsourcers are all byzantine, right? or there is one outsourcer that is byzantine) <dankrad> ok, but what stops generalized outsourcers from appearing? <n0ble> because his business is build on ethereum and it’s better to stay honest and make money rather than compormise security. probably i am wrong. though, random “outsourcer” could favour compromising security for isntant revenue (re @dankrad: why would the outsourcer not give you anything?) <vbuterin> right, they can easily appear <vbuterin> But this isn't an eth2 specific thing <vbuterin> Outsourcing will happen regardless of what we do <dankrad> right, but currently all nodes on the Eth1 p2p net fully validate the chain <dankrad> so an invalid block would be weeded out pretty quickly <vbuterin> right, so I'm saying we don't have to actually build the code for stateless validation until we add a proof of custody <n0ble> this is done by users <n0ble> we have a fistful of miners and users which is similar to have a fistful of outsourcers and users <dankrad> An my worry is the time before stateless validation when we have the worst case of verifier dilemma ever (re @vbuterin: right, so I'm saying we don't have to actually build the code for stateless validation until we add a proof of custody) <vbuterin> Wait I am really confused here <vbuterin> Isn't this true precisely because we do not yet have stateless validation? (re @dankrad: right, but currently all nodes on the Eth1 p2p net fully validate the chain) <dankrad> no it's not equivalent, because all miners are currently fully validating. whereas by separating Eth2 consensus from Eth1 validation, I can see a situation arising where a supermajority of consensus nodes are not actually validating the eth1 state transition (re @n0ble: we have a fistful of miners and users which is similar to have a fistful of outsourcers and users) <dankrad> Not sure what you are trying to say? Do we agree that most likely we will do merge before statelessness? (re @vbuterin: Isn't this true precisely because we do not yet have stateless validation?) <vbuterin> yes <vbuterin> But until we have statelessness, where's the verifier's dilemma? <vbuterin> You have to verify to keep an updated state <dankrad> what's the incentive to verify eth1 state transition? <vbuterin> Do we agree that the answer to this question does NOT change just from the merge itself (assuming the merge does not enable statelessness)? (re @dankrad: what's the incentive to verify eth1 state transition?) <dankrad> it does, because consensus is more distributed. The verification cost is trivial to miners and it is not to stakers <vbuterin> ah I see <dankrad> also, I don't see non-validator P2P notes doing any validation <vbuterin> poor man's PoC: maker of block N chooses k addresses, maker of block N+1 must provide the balances of those addresses 😂 <dankrad> yeah I was thinking about that. Just PoC the eth1 state <dankrad> that is probably the easiest solution that will require to maintain it fully <dankrad> but you need attesters to do it as well <dankrad> otherwise a dishonest proposer can DOS the chain <n0ble> it’s not an equivalent but in the model where block producers doesn’t get any rewards (i.e. transaction fees) if the other producer has discarded an invalid block it does look pretty similar to me, except for absence of extra rewards paid to miners. Unless we need a supercomputer to produce an eth1 block and and verify that the state root is correct which would be a single point of failuer, cryptoeconomics should handle it. Please, point out to the place where I am starting to get wrong (re @dankrad: no it's not equivalent, because all miners are currently fully validating. whereas by separating Eth2 consensus from Eth1 validation, I can see a situation arising where a supermajority of consensus nodes are not actually validating the eth1 state transition) <n0ble> PoC is definitely a good improve

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content:
<dankrad> The problem is that for the executable beacon chain, we want *every* staker to run an Eth1 node, otherwise security will really be much worse (because we can get a majority chain on an incorrect Eth1 state transition otherwise, and we don't even have fraud proofs to stop it)

This is different once we have weak statelessness, because then running the Eth1 node will be cheap (only need to verify a block every now and then, not maintain state); and producing blocks will be much more expensive (need to run a stateful Eth1 node), so outsourcing makes a lot of sense and won't compromise security (re @n0ble: there should be an equilibrium between cost of running own eth1 node and transaction fees that the owner of the node can make. It’s a centralisation risk of course. But I believe staking pools will run their own eth1 nodes while home stakers would rather outsource eth1 node responsibilities to someone else. The latter also contributes to the promise of running validator on average laptop and raspberri pi)

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content:
<dankrad> Just see the difference:
Current situation: Miners verify the state transitions. Miners invest millions in hardware and infrastructure, operational costs are similar to rewards. You can assume they have at least 10k+ operations cost per month, but most are likely only profitable at 1M+. State verification needs a single Eth1 node for them, which has a running cost of maybe 10-100$ per month. If they don't do it, they risk their blocks being orphaned, which is losing 1000s of $ per block.
Post-merge: Validators verify the state transitions. The operational cost of running a validator at home is cost of hardware (can get it for <200$) plus electricity and internet connection (<50$/month). Adding a full Eth1 node costs maybe 500$ in hardware and doubles your electricity cost. So not trivial at all. In my case, I eventually outsourced Eth1 to a dedicated server because it just clogged up my internet connection too much (which to be fair wouldn't be a problem if you're only doing verification)
Cost of not verifying: You may very occasionally vote for the wrong head, if someone produces an incorrect block. Each (very rare) time this happens you would lose $0.01 (one cent) in rewards at current prices
